explanation:
## The gate

```systemverilog
assign found_out = found_in &  armed;
assign missed    = found_in & ~armed;

always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    if (!rst_n)                 armed <= 1'b0;
    else if (arm)               armed <= 1'b1;
    else if (found_in && armed) armed <= 1'b0;
end
```

Five lines, and both of the interesting decisions are visible in them.

**The outputs are combinational.** `found_out` is about this cycle.
Registering it would put the count a cycle behind the detection and
break the correspondence between `found` and `count` that milestone 2
established.

**The priority chain is the specification.** An if/else-if chain in a
clocked block is a priority encoder: the first true branch wins. Put
`arm` above the self-disarm and a pulse coinciding with a passed
detection leaves the gate armed; swap them and it does not. Both are
perfectly implementable, and which one you get is decided by the order
of two lines — which is why the specification states it rather than
leaving it to be discovered.

The grading testbench separates the cases directly: it arms the gate on
the cycle a match is passing and then feeds two more matches. With
`arm` winning, two get through; without, one.

## Two instances of one module

```systemverilog
det_counter #(.W(W)) u_count  (.clk(clk), .rst_n(rst_n), .inc(found),
                               .count(count), .sat(sat));
det_counter #(.W(W)) u_missed (.clk(clk), .rst_n(rst_n), .inc(missed),
                               .count(missed_count), .sat());
```

Each instance is its own hardware — its own register, its own adder —
and they share nothing but the source text. That is the whole argument
for having written `det_counter` as a module in milestone 2 rather than
putting a counter inline in the top: the second one cost one line.

`.sat()` leaves an output unconnected on purpose. It is legal, it is
explicit, and it is better than a wire nothing reads.

## Where the arm pulse lands, and why

This is the part that catches people, and it follows directly from the
registered output chosen in milestone 1.

```
cycle:       n-3  n-2  n-1    n     n+1
din:          1    0    1     1      x
hist(after):  ..1 ..10 .101  1011   ....
found:        0    0    0     0      1     <- one cycle after the last bit
```

The last bit is clocked in at the edge ending cycle `n`; `found` is set
by that same edge, so it is high during cycle `n+1`. An arm pulse "on
the same cycle as the detection" is a pulse during cycle `n+1`.

Had the detector been combinational — `assign found = (hist == pattern)`
— every piece of timing downstream would shift by a cycle. The decision
made in the first milestone is still being paid for in the third, which
is how interfaces usually work.

## What the pair of counters buys

One count says how many detections were acted on; the other says how
many arrived while nobody was listening. Together they survive
saturation of either: the grading testbench runs a stream with ten
matches into three-bit counters, and the missed count sits at 7 saying
"at least seven" — true and useful, where a wrapping counter would have
said 2.
